title: Elodie and the Letter
premise: In the aftermath of the Vellmore Campaign, battlefield nurse Kestrel Coldharbour has spent six years quietly recording in his private ledger the names of soldiers erased from official dispatches—men sacrificed by officers who preferred clean reports to true ones. When a census taker named Elodie Ferris arrives asking questions his answers can't survive, she recognizes what he is and forces a choice: bury the ledger forever, or testify before a commission that the victors' historians are already rewriting. As Kestrel's found family of veterans, widows, and fellow record-keepers rallies around him, he must race to get the truth on the public record before the century turns and the last witnesses die or disperse. The book ends with Kestrel reading the ledger aloud into the commission's transcript, Elodie at his side, knowing justice came too late for most—but not, finally, for the names themselves.
about_author: August Blackwood is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing military correspondence in provincial record offices. They write historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Six years after the war, Kestrel lives quietly as a village apothecary's assistant, tending wounds and adding names to a hidden ledger of soldiers the officers' reports omitted. A visit from an old comrade's widow reminds him why he keeps it. Emotional beat: guarded tenderness; the past is close but contained.

chapters.title: A Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Census taker Elodie Ferris arrives with her official forms, but her questions drift from household size to service records to a battle Kestrel claims he never saw. He lies badly; she notices everything. Emotional beat: first crack in the armor—the terror of being seen.

chapters.title: What Elodie Carries
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie reveals she lost a brother at Vellmore whose name appears on no memorial, and that she has been tracing omitted men across three counties. She doesn't threaten Kestrel—she simply shows him her own list. Emotional beat: recognition between two keepers of the dead.

chapters.title: The Commission Announced
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. News breaks: a Royal Commission on War Records will sit through winter, ostensibly to 'correct clerical errors.' The victors' historians are preparing a sanitized official history. Kestrel realizes his ledger could either correct the record or destroy him as a forger. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Apothecary's Cellar
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. Kestrel gathers his found family: Sergeant Bram Tull, who drinks to forget; Mrs. Halloway, who lost three sons; young Tam, a deserter Kestrel sheltered. He shows them the ledger for the first time. Emotional beat: fragile trust—the family forms around a shared secret.

chapters.title: Colonel Ashgrave Comes Home
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Colonel Ashgrave, the officer whose dispatches omitted the most names, returns to the district as a decorated hero advising the Commission. He pays Kestrel a courteous, chilling visit, making clear he knows about 'the nurse who writes things down.' Emotional beat: cold fear; the enemy has a face and manners.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Old Debt
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram begs Kestrel to stay silent—not from cowardice but because testifying would brand Tam a deserter and expose Mrs. Halloway's forged pension papers. Loyalty pulls one way, truth the other. Emotional beat: love weaponized as an argument for silence.

chapters.title: The Widow's Testimony
chapters.summary: Mrs. Halloway's POV. Against advice, Mrs. Halloway speaks at the Commission's open session and is publicly humiliated by Ashgrave's counsel as hysterical and mistaken. Kestrel watches, ledger heavy beneath his coat, and does nothing. Emotional beat: shame—the cost of waiting.

chapters.title: Elodie's Bargain
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie offers Kestrel a deal: she has a contact inside the Commission who will enter verified testimony into the permanent record, but only if Kestrel can corroborate names with dates, units, and witnesses—and only if he accepts legal exposure. Emotional beat: hope arriving dressed as risk.

chapters.title: Copying by Candlelight
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam, who can barely write, spends nights copying the ledger into fair hand while Kestrel dictates, the two growing close as father and son. A near-discovery by a lodger nearly ends everything. Emotional beat: warmth and terror braided together; the ledger becomes inheritance.

chapters.title: Ashgrave's Countermove
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Ashgrave strikes first: Kestrel is accused of falsifying medical records during the war, and his apothecary license is suspended pending inquiry. The message is clear—testify and be destroyed. Emotional beat: the trap closing; isolation.

chapters.title: The Patients Speak
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. The found family refuses to let Kestrel stand alone: former patients, nurses, and conscripts begin arriving unbidden to vouch for him, each carrying their own fragment of the truth. Emotional beat: the turning point—he was never invisible; he was beloved.

chapters.title: Bram's Confession
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram reveals he was the surviving officer of the Vellmore rear guard and signed the order abandoning the wounded whose names Kestrel keeps. He offers to testify against himself if Kestrel will read the ledger aloud. Emotional beat: guilt transmuted into courage; loyalty and truth reconciled.

chapters.title: The Stolen Dispatch
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie risks her position to retrieve the original Vellmore dispatch from the Commission's own archive, proving the omissions were deliberate edits, not clerical error. She is caught, dismissed, and served with a warrant. Emotional beat: sacrifice; the cost made flesh.

chapters.title: Night Before the Commission
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. On the eve of the hearing, the family gathers: ledger copied, witnesses sworn, Elodie bailed into Kestrel's custody. Kestrel reads every name aloud once, privately, so no one hears them first as evidence—they hear them first as people. Emotional beat: solemn consecration.

chapters.title: The Hearing, Part One
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel takes the stand. Ashgrave's counsel dismantles his credibility piece by piece until Kestrel abandons defense and simply begins reading names—four hundred and eleven of them—while the hall falls silent. Emotional beat: climax begins; truth as sheer endurance.

chapters.title: The Hearing, Part Two
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. Bram corroborates the abandonments at the cost of confessing his own crime; Mrs. Halloway identifies her sons among the names; Tam testifies to what deserters saw. Ashgrave, cornered, invokes his service decorations. Emotional beat: the family's loyalty becomes the evidence itself.

chapters.title: Ashgrave Breaks
chapters.summary: Ashgrave's POV. Facing Bram's confession and the altered dispatch, Ashgrave collapses—not into remorse but into contempt, insisting history belongs to victors. The Commission chairman, himself a veteran of Vellmore, orders the ledger entered into the permanent record verbatim. Emotional beat: victory without triumph; some men never bend.

chapters.title: Sentences and Settlements
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Bram receives a reduced sentence for his confession; Kestrel's charges are dropped but his license is not restored; Elodie faces trial for the stolen dispatch. Justice outside the law proves partial, imperfect, real. Emotional beat: bittersweet accounting.

chapters.title: Elodie's Own Name
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. At her hearing, Kestrel and the whole found family testify for her; the Commission, wary of further scandal, releases her with a reprimand. She asks Kestrel, almost shyly, whether the ledger has room for one more keeper. Emotional beat: love arriving without announcement.

chapters.title: The Century Turns
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. On New Year's Eve 1899, the village gathers as the amended roll of the Vellmore dead is read publicly for the first time, Elodie's brother's name among them. Kestrel adds a final entry: not a soldier, but a date, and the words 'they were counted.' Emotional beat: release; grief given its public shape.

chapters.title: Elodie and the Letter
chapters.summary: Epilogue, dual POV. Years later, Elodie finds the letter Kestrel wrote the night before the hearing—never sent—confessing his fear and his hope. They read it together by the fire, the ledger now a printed appendix carried in other hands, other counties. Emotional beat: quiet permanence; the record outlives them all.
